proposed statement: The co-op aims to calculate advance payments to growers based on monthly fruit packout data
key statement: Sipho's spreadsheet has a row per delivery and is used to calculate monthly advance payments per carton of class one and two and per bin of juice, with a final pool payment once a year in February; payments go out via a bank batch file and the totals are journalled into LedgerOne monthly.

proposed statement: The co-op has a complex payment process with advance payments and a final pool payment that occurs once a year

proposed statement: The weighbridge must keep working without the network to prevent trucks from waiting at the gate, which would cause fruit to sit in the sun for up to twenty trucks
key statement: Intake at the weighbridge must keep working without the network and catch up when the link is back; trucks can never be stopped at the gate.

proposed statement: The Optisort grader system is locked down with a password that the client does not have, and the supplier requires a password to be reset before providing access
key statement: The Optisort grader's computer is locked down, its reports are PDFs and touching it would void the support contract, so getting packout data out automatically is uncertain and could slip; if it does, Marietjie keeps typing for a while.

proposed statement: The client currently calculates payments using a spreadsheet that generates a batch file for bank transfers, and they do not want to move this to the new system in phase one
key statement: The advance payment calculation stays in Sipho's spreadsheet for phase one, because the board changes the rates every season; the new system supplies the deliveries and packout as an export.

proposed statement: The weighbridge tablet should only store day's deliveries and grower list, not bank details
key statement: The weighbridge tablet needs a PIN or login and holds only what it needs (the day's deliveries and the grower list, not bank details), in case it is stolen.

proposed statement: Growers have varying phone usage: big farmers use iPhones and laptops, small growers use cheap Android phones with expensive data
key statement: Growers' pages must work on cheap Android phones over slow connections without using much data, as a web page opened from a link (savable to the home screen), not an app to download.

proposed statement: Growers keep financial records for five years in boxes in the storeroom where mice eat some of them
key statement: Deliveries and statements are kept for five years (the auditors' rule), including for growers who leave.

proposed statement: The system must work on cheap Android phones with slow connections without eating data
key statement: Growers' pages must work on cheap Android phones over slow connections without using much data, as a web page opened from a link (savable to the home screen), not an app to download.

proposed statement: Growers should receive SMS notifications when their batch is graded with delivery numbers and class percentages
key statement: When a batch is graded, the grower gets an SMS with the packout (for example 78% class one) and a link; SMS first, WhatsApp perhaps later. Ruan thinks an SMS costs about 25 to 30 cents.

proposed statement: Growers change phone numbers, so the system must update phone numbers through the office like bank details
key statement: Bank details, and growers' phone numbers, are changed only by the office (bank details by Sipho with a letter from the bank), never by the grower from their phone, after an attempted fraud last year.

proposed statement: The weighbridge tablet may break on busy mornings, so carbon books are kept as backup
key statement: Intake prints a small slip for each grower on the truck for the driver to take away; the carbon books stay as a fallback if the tablet fails, with a quick way to enter those tickets afterwards.

proposed statement: The weighbridge process requires splitting one truck's weight across multiple growers by the number of bins each grower has on the truck
key statement: One truck can carry several growers' bins (a contractor collects from six or seven small growers); intake splits the truck's net weight across growers by number of bins, and each grower's ticket shows his share. The contractor, paid by the growers directly, needs nothing from the system.

proposed statement: The system must capture deliveries at the weighbridge in under a minute for the clerk to process
key statement: Capturing a delivery should take the clerk under a minute (it takes four to five minutes now, and the queue backs up onto the road).

proposed statement: The system must handle up to 2400 bins per day during peak season and 1800 bins per day during normal season
key statement: At the peak, 60 to 70 trucks a day, mostly between 07:00 and 11:00, carrying 6 to 40 bins each; 2,400 bins on the peak day last season and about 1,800 on a normal mid-season day.

proposed statement: The weighbridge process involves multiple growers sharing transport through a contractor who collects from several growers in one trip
key statement: One truck can carry several growers' bins (a contractor collects from six or seven small growers); intake splits the truck's net weight across growers by number of bins, and each grower's ticket shows his share. The contractor, paid by the growers directly, needs nothing from the system.

proposed statement: The system must handle the morning rush at the weighbridge and notifications after grading
key statement: Up to 162 member growers would use the portal (140 delivered last season; the others can come back any time), and the big farms have several users each (owner, manager, perhaps a bookkeeper), so a few hundred users at most.

proposed statement: The system must account for the fact that some growers share transport with other growers through a contractor
key statement: One truck can carry several growers' bins (a contractor collects from six or seven small growers); intake splits the truck's net weight across growers by number of bins, and each grower's ticket shows his share. The contractor, paid by the growers directly, needs nothing from the system.

proposed statement: The system must handle the fact that the number of growers is growing at a rate of 10% per year for the next five years
key statement: Volume is growing: two new members are planting, and navel orchards are being replaced with mandarins (smaller fruit, more cartons per bin); the board's plan is 10% more volume a year for the next five years, though Johan isn't sure it will happen.

proposed statement: The system must allow the weighbridge clerks to use the WeighMate screen
key statement: At the weighbridge, a rugged tablet rather than the PC, with big buttons usable with gloves and a screen readable in the sun; at the tipper, as close to one button as possible.

proposed statement: The system must allow the weighbridge clerks to use the WeighMate screen
key statement: Packhouse users: two weighbridge clerks (one per shift, both together in the peak) and three tipper staff over the shifts, plus Precious and the foreman; the clerks are comfortable with WhatsApp and the WeighMate screen, the tipper staff less so.

proposed statement: The system must have a single button for the tipper operators

proposed statement: The client currently uses a spreadsheet for monthly reports on volumes, packout, and advances paid
key statement: The board's monthly report (volumes, packout, advances paid), which takes Sipho a day by hand, stays in his spreadsheet in phase one, with the volumes and packout coming from the system.

proposed statement: The project must be completed before the end of February to prepare for the mandarin harvest
key statement: Weighbridge intake live by 1 March 2027 (first mandarins at the end of March); grower pages by the end of April 2027.

proposed statement: The system must allow the weighbridge clerks to practice with made-up deliveries in February to prepare for the season
key statement: Training in February with practice days on made-up deliveries: two sessions for the packhouse team (shifts) and one for the office; a short manual with pictures; the consultant on site for the first two mornings of the season.

proposed statement: The weighbridge intake must be live by the first of March 2027 to handle the first mandarins

proposed statement: The system must provide a way for growers to see last season's deliveries for comparison
key statement: The grower list with its orchard blocks and cultivars (about 600 blocks, partly out of date, checked by Marietjie) is brought over from the spreadsheet; last season's deliveries only if cheap, to be decided once the consultant has seen the spreadsheet.

proposed statement: The system must allow the weighbridge clerks to practice with made-up deliveries in February to prepare for the season
key statement: Training in February with practice days on made-up deliveries: two sessions for the packhouse team (shifts) and one for the office; a short manual with pictures; the consultant on site for the first two mornings of the season.

key statement: Does the grower see the packout straight from the grader, or only after Precious has checked the report (which would make her a bottleneck at about 60 batches a day in the peak)?

proposed statement: The system must work with the existing Wi-Fi infrastructure that has limited coverage in degreening rooms
key statement: The Wi-Fi doesn't reach inside the degreening rooms (insulated panel walls); scanning at their doors would need another outdoor access point, about R5,000 to R6,000 with cabling.

proposed statement: The client needs to track cartons packed per cultivar and class for the export agent, who requires this data by Monday morning to plan shipments.
key statement: The cold store (pallets with their own numbers, tracked in the cold store manager's book) stays out of phase one; the agent will probably want it later.

key statement: The cold store (pallets with their own numbers, tracked in the cold store manager's book) stays out of phase one; the agent will probably want it later.

proposed statement: The client has a problem with growers sharing phone numbers, which affects how the system handles multiple growers under one number.
key statement: When several growers share one phone (for example the Mathebula family, three grower numbers on one phone), does whoever has the phone see all of them, or does each grower need his own number? Sipho will ask the lawyer member.

proposed statement: The client has a statement that includes packing fees, bin hire, transport costs, levies, and previous month's payments for comparison.
key statement: Statements show the advance less deductions: a packing fee per carton, bin hire for co-op bins (R35 per bin per season), transport for the few who use the co-op's truck, and levies, with last month next to this month; Sipho will send a sample with a fake name.

proposed statement: The client uses WhatsApp for communication with big farms but not small growers, which affects their ability to plan the line.
key statement: Big farms could optionally give notice on their page of the bins coming the next day (they now WhatsApp Precious), to help plan the line; a nice-to-have for a later phase unless cheap, and never compulsory.

proposed statement: The client loses about a hundred bins annually due to them being misplaced or lost

proposed statement: The client wants to see what growers will see before building the system
key statement: See the main grower screens designed first and reviewed with some growers before anything is built, and a half-hour progress update every two weeks showing working software, not slides.

proposed statement: The client requires a person to manage system day-to-day operations including adding growers and clerks
key statement: Who at the co-op looks after the system day to day (adding growers and clerks, resetting tablets)? Perhaps Marietjie's replacement; Johan will come back on it before training.
